Not quite, friend. David really does list it: "the one anointed by the God of Jacob" (2 Samuel 23:1). It's right there in the middle of his titles. He's saying God is the One who set him apart, and he's not bragging about it.

That's the one. David says, "The Spirit of the LORD spoke through me; His word was on my tongue." (2 Samuel 23:2). He's the mouth and God is the message. A good messenger knows the difference, and David sure does.

Nathan, the prophet who spoke to David in his day (2 Samuel 12:1), is a good guess, friend. But David names someone else here. He says, "The Spirit of the LORD spoke through me; His word was on my tongue." (2 Samuel 23:2). These words came straight through David himself.

Jesse is in the first verse, so I see how he got picked. David calls himself "David son of Jesse" (2 Samuel 23:1). But Jesse isn't the one speaking through him. David says, "The Spirit of the LORD spoke through me" (2 Samuel 23:2). Jesse only shows up as the name on David's family line.

explanations.answer: With justice and in the fear of God
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. The Rock of Israel says the ruler is the one "who rules the people with justice, who rules in the fear of God" (2 Samuel 23:3). Two things, and both are about how he rules. Nothing in there about how big the castle is.

explanations.answer: With a strong army and high walls
explanations.explanation: Army and walls sound like a ruler's whole to-do list, don't they? But God doesn't mention either one. The ruler is the one "who rules the people with justice, who rules in the fear of God" (2 Samuel 23:3). The verse is about how he rules, not what he builds.

explanations.answer: With great riches and many allies
explanations.explanation: Riches and allies look impressive, friend. But that's not what God lists. He says the ruler is the one "who rules the people with justice, who rules in the fear of God" (2 Samuel 23:3). No treasure chest anywhere in the verse.

explanations.answer: Like morning light at a cloudless dawn
explanations.explanation: Yes! God says that ruler "is like the light of the morning at sunrise of a cloudless dawn" (2 Samuel 23:4). Picture that first light with not one cloud in the way. That's the picture God chose for a ruler who rules with justice.

explanations.answer: Like a cedar standing tall in the forest
explanations.explanation: A cedar is a handsome tree, friend, but it's not in this verse. God says the ruler "is like the light of the morning at sunrise of a cloudless dawn" (2 Samuel 23:4). His picture is about light coming up, and a tree standing there doesn't fit it.

explanations.answer: Like a wall around a strong city
explanations.explanation: A wall makes sense if you're thinking about keeping people safe. But God picks a different picture. He says the ruler "is like the light of the morning at sunrise of a cloudless dawn" (2 Samuel 23:4). It's a sunrise, not a fortress.

Careful, baker, this one slipped by. The grass in God's picture isn't dry at all. The verse says "the glistening after the rain on the sprouting grass of the earth" (2 Samuel 23:4). It's fresh, wet and sprouting after the rain.

That's right. God's picture has "the glistening after the rain on the sprouting grass of the earth" (2 Samuel 23:4). So the grass has just had rain and it's sprouting. No dry, crunchy grass in this one.

You've got it. David says, "He has established with me an everlasting covenant, ordered and secured in every part." (2 Samuel 23:5). Everlasting means it doesn't run out. David is pretty sure of it, and I'd say with good reason.

Not this time, friend. David says plainly, "For He has established with me an everlasting covenant, ordered and secured in every part." (2 Samuel 23:5). The word is everlasting. He's not talking about a short-term deal.

explanations.answer: His full salvation and every desire
explanations.explanation: That's it. David asks, "Will He not bring about my full salvation and my every desire?" (2 Samuel 23:5). He's asking it right after talking about the covenant, so he's leaning on God's promise. The man is feeling sure about it.

explanations.answer: A long and peaceful old age
explanations.explanation: A quiet old age sounds lovely, baker, I'd take one myself. But David doesn't say that here. He asks, "Will He not bring about my full salvation and my every desire?" (2 Samuel 23:5). He's looking for something bigger than a comfy rocking chair.

David was a warrior, so I get why you went there. But victory over neighbors isn't what he mentions. He asks, "Will He not bring about my full salvation and my every desire?" (2 Samuel 23:5). It's about salvation and what he truly desires.

Sand on the seashore is a different picture than David's, friend. He says, "the worthless are all like thorns raked aside" (2 Samuel 23:6). Thorns have prickles and sand doesn't. Sand also won't hurt your hands the way thorns will.

That's right. David says these thorns "can never be gathered by hand" (2 Samuel 23:6). Nobody's scooping them up with bare hands. Anybody who's grabbed a thorny branch knows why.
Iron it is, friend. The man who touches them "must be armed with iron or with the shaft of a spear" (2 Samuel 23:7). That's some serious gear just to handle thorns. It tells you how prickly they are.

Cloth feels like a reasonable guess, but it's no match for thorns. David says the man must be armed "with iron or with the shaft of a spear" (2 Samuel 23:7). Iron is the right word here. Cloth would be shredded.

Reeds are too bendy to do the job, baker. David says the man "must be armed with iron or with the shaft of a spear" (2 Samuel 23:7). So the word is iron. Hard metal and a spear shaft, not something that would snap.
Not quite, baker. David says, "The fire burns them to ashes in the place where they lie." (2 Samuel 23:7). They aren't hauled anywhere. They get burned right where they are.
Correct. David says, "The fire burns them to ashes in the place where they lie." (2 Samuel 23:7). So no long trip. They burn right where they lie, and that's how the poem ends.
